title: Home Safety Checklist for Older Adults: What to Check Room by Room
summary: Discover 13 household tasks seniors can delegate, from cleaning and repairs to yard work and snow removal, to make aging at home safer and easier.
body_markdown:
Good home safety for seniors comes down to five areas: entrances and exits, lighting, fall prevention, mobility, and emergency preparedness. This elderly home safety checklist covers all five. Work through them room by room and you'll find most of what needs attention in an afternoon. For the jobs you can't do yourself,[GoGo Home Services](https://www.gogograndparent.com/services/home-services-for-seniors) can connect you with a local handyman, electrician, or plumber on1 (855) 464-6872 .


If you're visiting a parent this autumn, it's a good time to do it. The months ahead bring dark afternoons, wet paths, and more time spent indoors, and a checklist for elderly living alone is easier to work through before the weather turns than after something happens.


## **Why does home safety for seniors matter so much?**


Falls are the reason. The CDC reports that[more than one in four older adults falls each year](https://www.cdc.gov/falls/data-research/facts-stats/index.html) , and about 37% of those who fall report an injury that needed medical treatment or kept them from their usual activities for at least a day. Falls are also the[leading cause of injury-related death](https://www.cdc.gov/falls/data-research/index.html) for adults over 65, which is why home safety for seniors is worth an afternoon of your time. Each year there are roughly 4.5 million emergency department visits and nearly 319,000 hospitalizations for hip fractures.


Falls have many causes, including medication, eyesight, balance and muscle strength, so the house is only part of it. But many of the common hazards inside a home are inexpensive to fix: a rug that slides, a dark stairwell, a missing grab bar. Good home safety for seniors is mostly small things done before they matter.


## **What should you check at the entrances?**


Start at the front door. Your parent should be able to get in and out easily, even in the dark or in bad weather.


1. **Light the pathway.** Motion-activated lights on the approach remove the guesswork when they're coming home after dark.
2. **Check the surface.** Non-slip paths matter most where it rains or freezes. Look for moss, loose slabs, and cracks.
3. **Test the locks.** A lock that sticks is a problem when someone's hands are cold or arthritic.
4. **Add a one-way peephole** so they can see who's there without opening up.
5. **Look at shelter.** A covered porch means they're not hunting for keys in the rain.
6. **Check accessibility.** Ramps for a wheelchair or walker are among the home modifications for seniors that pay off for years.
7. **Move the mailbox if it's awkward.** No stretching, no steps down to the curb.
8. **Consider an emergency button near the door** , which is one of the more useful additions to any checklist for elderly living alone.


## **Is the lighting good enough?**


Poor lighting sits behind a lot of falls, and better lighting is also one of the easiest improvements to make. It is usually where you see results fastest.


1. **Motion-sensor nightlights** in the bathroom, bedroom, and hallway, for the trip nobody plans at 3am.
2. **Task lighting** where they read, cook, or do anything fiddly.
3. **Stairs lit from above and along the steps** , so each tread is visible going down.
4. **A lit closet** , which sounds trivial until you've watched someone dress in the dark.
5. **Bedside light with a reachable switch** , so they're never crossing a dark room to reach the wall.
6. **Battery or rechargeable emergency lights** in the main rooms for power cuts.
7. **Adjustable brightness** , including warmer bulbs in the evening, which some people find easier on the eyes.


## **How do you prevent falls at home?**


Fall prevention is one of the most important parts of the checklist, and many of the fixes cost very little.


1. **Deal with the rugs.** Non-slip pads or double-sided tape, and take up anything that bunches. Sometimes removing a rug is the right answer.
2. **Non-slip mats in and outside the bath.** One of the cheapest home modifications for seniors with the biggest effect.
3. **Grab bars by the toilet and in the shower.** Fitted into studs, not just drywall anchors. The bathroom is also where a regular[cleaning routine](https://www.gogograndparent.com/blog/how-can-a-disabled-person-get-help-for-house-cleaning) does the most for safety.
4. **Handrails on both sides of every staircase** , not just one.
5. **Check the footwear.** Supportive shoes with real grip indoors. Socks on hard floors are a common culprit.
6. **Look at the chairs.** Sturdy, with armrests, and not so low or soft that standing up is a struggle.
7. **Clear the clutter** , particularly in hallways and on stair landings.
8. **Consider fall detection.** A wearable that alerts you matters most for anyone living alone.


If you'd rather not work through it yourself, GoGo Home Services can connect you with a local professional to look at the house and handle the jobs on this list.


## **Which home modifications for seniors make the biggest difference?**


Structural home modifications for seniors take more time and money than the items above. For someone planning to stay put, they are usually worth it.


1. **Ramps** for wheelchair or walker access.
2. **Lever handles instead of doorknobs.** Much easier to use when grip strength or arthritis makes twisting difficult, and inexpensive to fit.
3. **Lower cabinets and counters** , so things are reachable from a seat.
4. **Bathroom changes** , including a raised toilet seat and a walk-in shower.
5. **Wider doorways** where a walker has to fit through.
6. **Rearranged storage.** Daily items at waist height, at the front. No bending, no stretching.
7. **Bed height and position** , with a rail if getting up is difficult and space to move around it.
8. **Remote-controlled blinds** , which remove another reach-and-pull job.


The best changes are the ones that suit the person rather than the ones that look most thorough on paper. A walk-in shower matters more than a ramp if nobody uses a wheelchair.


## **Is your loved one ready for an emergency?**


Emergency preparedness is easy to postpone because you hope you'll never need it. That's exactly why it belongs on the checklist.


1. **Smoke and carbon monoxide alarms** , tested, with batteries changed on a schedule you actually keep.
2. **A fire extinguisher they can lift** , and an escape route you've both walked through.
3. **An emergency contact list** somewhere obvious. On the fridge, not in a drawer.
4. **A kit that covers three days:** water, non-perishable food, medications, first aid, flashlight and batteries, blankets, a phone charger, and copies of ID and medical records.
5. **Pet supplies** , if there's an animal in the house.
6. **Local emergency alerts** , registered on their phone or landline.
7. **A medical alert system** that reaches emergency services and you.


## **How often should you go through the checklist?**


Home safety for seniors isn't a one-off. Things drift. A bulb goes, a rug moves back, a handrail loosens.


A short walk through the house each month catches most of it, and once a year go through the whole checklist properly. Early autumn is a sensible time to make that the habit, before the weather starts creating its own hazards.

## **Working through the checklist**


A safer home usually comes down to catching small problems early. Work through the checklist once carefully, check the basics every month, and bring in professional help for anything you can't safely handle yourself.


Many of the changes on this list are simple and inexpensive, while the larger modifications can be tackled as needed. That's usually what lets a parent stay in the home they want to be in.


## **Frequently Asked Questions**


### **What should be on a home safety checklist for elderly living alone?**


A good checklist for elderly living alone covers five areas: entrances and exits, lighting, fall prevention, mobility and accessibility, and emergency preparedness. Start with fall prevention, then lighting, which is usually the quickest to improve.


### **What are the most important home modifications for seniors?**


Grab bars in the bathroom, handrails on both sides of the stairs, lever door handles instead of knobs, better lighting on stairs and in hallways, and removing or securing loose rugs. Most are inexpensive and quick to fit, and together they cover the bulk of the risk.


### **How common are falls among older adults?**


The CDC reports that more than one in four older adults falls each year, and about 37% of those who fall report an injury needing medical treatment or restricting their activity for at least a day. Falls lead to roughly 4.5 million emergency department visits annually, which is why fall prevention sits at the top of the checklist.


### **How often should I check my parent's home for safety?**


A quick walk through monthly, and the full checklist once a year. Things drift over time, so the monthly look matters more than people expect. Autumn is a practical time for the annual one, before darker afternoons and wet or icy paths arrive.
